UX research · Persona study

Alderwick Bank (fictional demo bank website)

People find the price in seconds and miss the conditions that change it: every quick decider left with the headline number and not the fee, cutoff or penalty behind it.

4 simulated personas · 6 walks (3 mobile, 3 desktop) · http://127.0.0.1:5188/
2026-11-21
At a glance2 of 6 walks reached a page that confirms their goal. 10 problems verified against the recordings (1 high, 5 medium, 4 low); start with F3 F1 F2. Simulated personas show where to look, not how many customers would struggle.

01Key insights

  1. Headline numbers are easy to find; the conditions that change them are not

    The comparison table, merchant card and rates table each answered the persona's question within 4–5 steps, and every persona stopped there. The 9 p.m. same-day cutoff, the $19.95/mo PCI fee, the per-cycle direct-deposit rule, the $3 paper-statement fee and the CD early-withdrawal penalty all sit a page deeper or at the foot of the page. Repeat walks stopped at the same places with the same doubts.

    Evidence F3 F2 F4
  2. Switchers nearly quit the application over a step that never blocks them

    Funding offers 'Fund within 30 days', and the re-walk reached Submit with no routing number. Nothing says so before step 4: the first walk saved for later at the Address step, and the second carried on only 'hopefully'.

    Evidence F1
  3. Three of four personas had to hunt in the menu for their part of the bank

    The home page speaks only to personal checking. The cafe owner, the CD shopper and the retiree each opened the hamburger menu to find business, rates or wealth; on a phone the hero and cookie box fill the first screen.

    Evidence F5
  4. The cautious retiree was won over, but left unsure she even qualifies

    A 'within one business day' promise, a morning call slot and narrow consent wording made Eleanor comfortable. No screen states a private-banking minimum, and the required consent checkbox border measures 1.52:1 against a 3:1 target.

    Evidence F7 F6

What's working, and should stay

  • Prices shown openly with no form: the merchant overview card gives percent plus cents and $0 monthly, which Luis called the best thing about the site.
  • The checking comparison table put monthly fees, waivers and $0 overdraft side by side; Dana picked her account from it on one screen.
  • The /rates page's section chips (CDs) took Marcus straight to the 12-month row in large green figures.
  • The wealth contact form says up front that a relationship manager will contact you within one business day, offers 'In the morning (8-11 a.m.)', and its consent covers only this request, which met Eleanor's 'not a sales trap' test.
  • The Funding step's 'Fund within 30 days - your account opens now' option let the switcher apply without her old bank's details, and the Review page summarised every step with Edit links.

02What to fix first

03Findings in detail

Ranked by severity. Each finding leads with what went wrong and the fix; the screens behind it follow. Every one was checked against the recorded screenshots.

F3Merchant overview shows 'Same day*' and '$0' monthly with the conditions left off the page

High severity · trust · /business/merchant-services · affects Luis, cafe owner · confidence high

Both merchant walks got their per-transaction prices from the Card Processing card on the overview (2.65% + 10c in person, 3.40% + 15c online, Monthly fee $0), which genuinely answers the question with no form. In both, the asterisk on 'Same day*' stayed unexplained: the page has no footnote for it, and its Important information covers only underwriting, card brands, the $25 chargeback and hardware tax. Both inferred the condition from the intro line and both left unsure whether they must open Alderwick business checking ('I think I can get next-day without banking here, but not sure'). The 9 p.m. ET cutoff and the $19.95/month PCI non-compliance fee are stated only on the Card Processing detail page (recon), which neither walk opened, so both concluded the monthly cost is $0 beyond the percentages while asking what a month would actually total; the second walk also found terminal prices ($349+) only in a separate card.

FixPut the asterisk's footnote under the card ('*Into Alderwick business checking for batches closed by 9 p.m. ET; next business day to any other bank - no Alderwick account required'), show the PCI non-compliance fee next to 'Monthly fee $0' ('$0; $19.95/mo only if PCI not validated'), and add a worked example ('$15,000 a month in person = about $X, plus a terminal from $349 if you need one').

Hit in 2 of 2 walks that reached /business/merchant-services.

F1The application doesn't say up front that funding can wait, so a switcher without her old bank's details may stop before she finds out

Medium severity · ux · /open?product=everyday-checking · affects Dana, nurse switching banks · confidence high

Step 1 shows only 'About 10 minutes - Secure application' and a five-step bar ending in Funding; nothing lists what to have ready or says funding can be done later. The Funding step does solve the problem: 'Fund within 30 days - Your account opens now; add money any time in the next 30 days' sits beside bank transfer and mailed check, and the re-walk (checking-switcher-3) chose it, finished all five steps and reached Submit without a routing number. So the first walk's fear was unfounded, but the site gave no way to know that early: in walk 1 Dana stopped at the Address step and saved for later because she expected Funding to demand her old bank's routing number; in walk 3 she pressed on only on hope ('funding is step 4 - hopefully skippable') and afterwards asked for a warning that the routing number is optional. Switchers, the audience for 'no overdraft fees', are the people least likely to have funding details at hand.

FixOn step 1, under 'About 10 minutes', add one line: 'You'll need ID and your SSN or ITIN. You can fund now or within 30 days, so no other bank details are needed to apply.' Show the 30-day option as a hint under Funding in the progress bar.

Hit in 2 of 2 walks that reached /open?product=everyday-checking.

F2The checking comparison table leaves out conditions and fees the product page states

Medium severity · copy · /compare/checking · affects Dana, nurse switching banks · confidence high

Both walks of Dana chose Everyday Checking from the comparison table alone and both asked whether the '$500 direct deposit' waiver is monthly; the table never says. The Everyday detail page (seen in recon, not by either walk) says 'each statement cycle' and lists a $3/month paper-statement fee that the table omits, so she twice left believing the waivable $10 fee was the only charge. The application's product card then summarises the waiver as 'or $0 with an easy waiver', which both walks called vague. People who decide from the table, which the home page sends them to, get a lossy version of the terms.

FixWrite the waiver row as '$500+ in direct deposits per statement cycle, or $1,500 daily balance, or age 17-24', add an 'Other fees' row (paper statements $3/month, $0 for e-statements or 65+), and replace 'easy waiver' on the application card with the actual waiver conditions.

Hit in 2 of 2 walks that reached /compare/checking, /open?product=everyday-checking.

F4The CD early-withdrawal penalty sits at the bottom of the rates page, past mortgages, loans and cards

Medium severity · friction · /rates · affects Marcus, saver checking rates · confidence high

Marcus found the 12-month rate (4.15%) and the $1,000 minimum within five taps, but the CD section's intro only says 'Fixed for the term'. The penalty (90 days of interest for terms of 12 months or less) is in the Important information at the foot of the page, below mortgages, personal loans and credit cards. On a phone one scroll took him past the CD table into mortgages, and he left without the penalty, one of the three things he needed before acting.

FixAdd the penalty to the CD intro line ('Fixed for the term. Early withdrawal: 90 days of interest for 12 months or less, 180 days for longer terms.') and link to /personal/cds.

Hit in 1 of 1 walks that reached /rates.

F5The home page speaks only to personal checking; business, wealth and rate seekers must find the menu

Medium severity · ux · / · affects Luis, cafe owner, Marcus, saver checking rates, Eleanor, recently retired executive · confidence medium

Three of the four personas (four of the six walks) came for something other than checking (card processing, a CD rate, private banking) and each reported the first screen had nothing for them: the badge, hero and buttons are all personal checking. On a phone the hero fills the first screen and the cookie box covers about a third of it on arrival. All recovered by opening the hamburger menu, so the cost was a moment of doubt ('Does this bank even have a private banking team?') rather than lost visits in this run. Dana, who wanted checking, went straight to 'Compare checking' and was unaffected.

FixAdd a row of entry points directly under the hero (Business banking and merchant services; Today's rates including the 12-month CD; Private banking, talk to a relationship manager), visible on the first phone screen once the cookie box is dismissed.

Hit in 4 of 6 walks that reached /; not by checking-switcher, checking-switcher-3.

F6The required consent checkbox on the wealth form has a near-invisible border

Medium severity · contrast · /wealth/contact · affects Eleanor, recently retired executive · confidence high

The 'I agree to be contacted' box, which must be ticked to send the request, has a pale grey border measured at 1.52:1 against white and is about 17 CSS px square. Eleanor (reading glasses, browsing at 150%) called it small and pale compared with everything else and wasn't sure the label was clickable too. She managed it, but a low-vision user can miss a required control and then hit an error on submit.

FixGive unchecked checkboxes and radios a border of at least 3:1 (for example the body grey #5c6c6c), enlarge the box to 24 px, and make the whole label a visible click target.

Measured 1.52:1 (#ccd3cd on #ffffff) against a target of 3.0:1, measurement retiree-wealth-callback:M1.[1, 2]

Hit in 1 of 1 walks that reached /wealth/contact.

F10The application page opens partway down and then jumps to the top, so the first tap misses

Low severity · ui · /open?product=everyday-checking · affects Dana, nurse switching banks · confidence low

In both checking walks, arriving from the comparison table's 'Open an account' showed the application already scrolled, with the heading half under the site header; the first tap on 'No' landed on the moving layout and missed, and the page then sat at the top. Each walk lost one tap and reported that the page jumped. It happened the same way twice, but a screenshot taken mid smooth-scroll would look identical, so part of it may be capture timing.

FixReset scroll to the top instantly (not smoothly) on route change, so /open first paints at the top.

Hit in 2 of 2 walks that reached /open?product=everyday-checking.

F7Nothing on the wealth path says who qualifies for private banking

Low severity · copy · /wealth/contact · affects Eleanor, recently retired executive · confidence medium

Eleanor, with about $2 million to move, asked repeatedly whether that was enough. The form asks for an asset band ('This helps us match you with the right team') but no screen she saw states a minimum or what happens below it. She completed the form anyway; the doubt lowered her confidence rather than stopping her.

FixState the private banking threshold, or 'There's no minimum to talk to us', beside the asset question and on the Wealth menu promo.

Hit in 1 of 1 walks that reached /wealth/contact.

F8Rate tables on a phone are cut off at the right edge with no sign they scroll

Low severity · ui · /rates · affects Marcus, saver checking rates · confidence medium

At 412 px wide the mortgage table's points column, the HELOC rate ('then 7.7...') and the credit card APRs ('variab...') are clipped at the right edge with no visible scroll cue. Marcus's CD table fit, so it didn't affect his task, but anyone on a phone comparing loans or cards would read partial figures.

FixStack those tables into cards below 600 px, or add a visible scroll shadow or label and keep the APR column in view.

Hit in 1 of 1 walks that reached /rates.

F9The site header hides the comparison table's column names while scrolling

Low severity · ui · /compare/checking · affects Dana, nurse switching banks · confidence high

When the comparison table is scrolled, its sticky column headings slide under the site's sticky header, so 'Interest Checking' and 'Student Checking' are half covered. Dana noticed and relied on column alignment to tell which 'Open an account' button was Everyday's. Only the first walk remarked on it; the re-walk scrolled the same table without comment.

FixOffset the table's sticky header by the site header's height (about 108 px on desktop) so column names stay fully visible.

Hit in 2 of 2 walks that reached /compare/checking.

04How each walk went

05Flow bottlenecks

Pages ranked by a score computed from the recordings: more steps, dead clicks, backtracking and exits on a page raise it.

06Accessibility measurements

Contrast and size were measured from screenshot pixels, not from the page's styles, and checked against WCAG 2.2: 4.5:1 for body text[1], 3:1 for large text and interface components[2], and a 24 × 24 CSS px minimum target[3].

07In their own words

6 of 6 personas gave an exit interview. Ease averaged 5.5 of 7, UMUX-Lite 74 of 100[4], satisfaction 4.0 of 5. On likelihood to recommend, 0 scored 9–10, 6 scored 7–8 and 0 scored 0–6. These are simulated answers, not a benchmark.

08What to test with real users

What these simulated walks can't settle, written as studies to run: the method, what to ask participants to do, who to recruit, and the result that would answer the question.

Q1Ask small-business owners on the merchant overview what they would pay per month on $15,000 of card sales and whether they expect any monthly fee; see whether anyone mentions PCI or the 9 p.m. cutoff.
Q2Watch bank switchers start the checking application without their old bank's details: does a step-1 note that funding can wait 30 days prevent early exits like walk 1's?
Q3Ask CD shoppers on phones, after using /rates, what it costs to withdraw early; check whether a penalty line next to the CD table is noticed.
Q4Watch low-vision users at 150-200% zoom complete the wealth form and note whether the consent checkbox is missed before submit.

09Who took part and how

Each persona used the site from screenshots alone and acted by clicking screen positions, with no access to page text, markup or accessibility names. A separate reviewer turned the recordings into findings; each one cites a session, a step and a box on that step's screenshot, and was re-checked against the recording before it was kept.[14]

Objective. Each persona completes their own task: open a checking account (/open), find card-processing pricing, request a relationship-manager conversation (/wealth/contact), or find the 12-month CD rate (/rates or a CD page). goal_match is the union of these pages because the driver takes one pattern per study.

10Limitations

  • These are simulated personas looking at screenshots. They show where to look, not how many real customers would struggle; counts are not rates.
  • Personas saw only pixels and the address bar: no page text, markup or accessibility tree. Screen-reader experience was not tested.
  • Contrast was measured from rendered pixels; anti-aliasing can shift a ratio slightly near a threshold.
  • Time estimates are the personas' own estimates per screen, not measured time on task.

Notes on this run

  • retiree-wealth-callback ended on the 30-step cap immediately after pressing 'Request a conversation'; checking-switcher-3 ended on the 45-step cap on 'Submit application'. Neither result screen was recorded, so whether either submission succeeded is unknown.
  • cafe-owner-merchant (walk 1) is marked claimed_goal_unverified only because goal_match then lacked /business/merchant-services; its step 5 screenshot shows the rates it reported, and the re-walk (cafe-owner-merchant-2) reached_goal on the same page.
  • checking-switcher-2 was discarded (its walker read the rendered report mid-walk) and is not used anywhere in this review.
  • /open's bottleneck score (53) is inflated by the walker: 30 steps per visitor come from one step per field click and typed value, and of its 8 dead clicks, steps 42-45 of checking-switcher-3 were checkbox ticks and the Submit press that did take effect (all three boxes are ticked at step 45) but changed too little of the screen for the change check. The other four are the two missed taps per walk in F10.
  • /wealth/contact's bottleneck score (30) likewise comes almost entirely from steps per visitor in field-by-field form filling; clarity averaged 4.7 and effort 1.2.
  • Exposure counts every walk of a named persona that reached the page as hit; for F9 only the first checking walk actually remarked on the problem.
  • The CD and wealth pages were each visited by one walk, so F4, F6, F7 and F8 rest on a single walk.
